# Future directions

The completed Lean development proves the local arithmetic dictionary for the quadratic
character `χ_D(p) = (D/p)`: ramification gives color `0`, and unramified primes split into
square/color `1` and nonsquare/color `-1` cases. It is uniform in every integer parameter
`D` and every prime `p`, so it applies in particular to every fundamental discriminant with
absolute value at most 1000.

The original mission's global claims are substantially larger than this local core. A faithful
next phase should proceed as follows.

1. **Fundamental discriminants.** Define the predicate characterizing quadratic-field
   discriminants (`D ≡ 1 mod 4` and squarefree, or `D = 4m` with the standard congruence
   and squarefreeness conditions), and prove uniqueness of the quadratic field attached to
   each such `D`.
2. **Certified bounded enumeration.** Construct a finite list of all fundamental
   discriminants satisfying `|D| ≤ 1000`, prove soundness and completeness of that list,
   and derive the exact count in Lean. This is the missing part of the proposed bounded test;
   no unchecked count is asserted here.
3. **Global Dirichlet characters.** Package the Kronecker symbol `n ↦ (D/n)` as a Mathlib
   `DirichletCharacter`, including the prime `2` and composite moduli. Prove its conductor is
   `|D|` for fundamental `D` and connect evaluation at odd primes to `quadraticColor`.
4. **Quadratic fields and Frobenius.** Formalize the quadratic extension `ℚ(√D)`, identify
   its Galois group with a two-element group, and prove the Frobenius splitting criterion at
   every unramified prime. This would turn the local Legendre-symbol classification into an
   explicit shape-to-color statement.
5. **Injectivity and surjectivity in the quadratic case.** Prove distinct fundamental
   discriminants yield distinct primitive quadratic Dirichlet characters, and conversely
   classify primitive quadratic characters by fundamental discriminants. This is the precise
   finite-order degree-one correspondence relevant to quadratic fields.
6. **Scope correction for higher rank.** The broad statement in the prompt—an unrestricted
   bijection between all irreducible representations of `Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ)` and cuspidal automorphic
   representations of `GL_n`—should not be used as a theorem without the customary
   continuity, semisimplicity, ramification, algebraicity, and compatibility hypotheses.
   Likewise, the modularity theorem concerns elliptic curves (and associated suitable
   two-dimensional representations), not every conceivable `n = 2` representation.

No OEIS sequence is needed for the uniform local theorem. If the certified bounded
fundamental-discriminant enumeration is completed, its ordered list or counting function can
then be compared against a relevant external sequence.

directions.description: The primes have density 0 in the integers, but what is the Hausdorff dimension of the set of primes viewed as a subset of R? Define the 'prime fractal' P as the set of primes with the metric d(p,q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|. This metric stretches out the primes so that the twin primes are close together and the large primes are spread out. Conjecture: The Hausdorff dimension dim_H(P, d) = 1. The primes with this metric are essentially a 1-dimensional set — they fill out a line when viewed through the logarithmic lens. This is because the prime number theorem pi(x) ~ x/log(x) means that in the d-metric, the 'length' of the primes up to x is sum_{p <= x} d(p, p+1) ~ sum_{p <= x} 1/(p*log(p)) ~ log(log(x)), which diverges. So the primes are 'long enough' to be 1-dimensional. But the Hausdorff dimension might be > 1 if the primes have fractal structure at small scales. In fact, dim_H(P, d) > 1 would mean the primes are more than a line — they have 'wrinkles' that fill more space. The twin prime conjecture predicts that there are infinitely many pairs of primes at d-distance ~ 1/(p*log(p)), creating a fractal dust that increases the dimension. Conjecture: dim_H(P, d) = 1 + epsilon where epsilon depends on the density of twin primes. If the twin prime conjecture is true, epsilon > 0. Test: estimate dim_H(P, d) by box-counting for primes up to 10^12 and verify it is close to 1 (or slightly above). Impact: the primes are a fractal with dimension 1 + epsilon, where epsilon measures the abundance of twin primes. If twin primes are infinite, the primes are more than a line — they are a fractal curve.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the metric d(p, q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)| on the set of primes P. Compute the Hausdorff dimension: dim_H(P, d) = lim_{delta -> 0} inf{sum r_i^s : P covered by balls of radius r_i < delta} where s is the infimum such that the sum is finite. By the prime number theorem, the interval [2, x] contains pi(x) ~ x/log(x) primes, and the d-length of this interval is 1/log(2) - 1/log(x) ~ 1/log(2). The 'average spacing' in the d-metric between consecutive primes near p is ~ 1/(p*log(p)^2). The box-counting dimension: N(epsilon) ~ (1/log(2)) / epsilon * (1/log(1/epsilon)) (number of boxes of size epsilon needed to cover P). So dim_box(P, d) = lim_{epsilon->0} log(N(epsilon))/log(1/epsilon) = 1 (since the log(1/epsilon) factor is sub-polynomial). For the Hausdorff dimension: if twin primes are infinite, the set of twin primes has accumulation points that may increase dim_H above 1. The key: the set of twin primes with the d-metric has dimension dim_H(twin primes, d) = 1/2 (since twin primes have density ~ C_2 * x/(log(x))^2 which gives s-measure finite for s > 1/2 and infinite for s < 1/2). So dim_H(P, d) = max(1, 1/2) = 1. The twin primes add a set of dimension 1/2 which does not increase the overall dimension. Conjecture: dim_H(P, d) = 1 exactly. Test: compute box-counting dimension numerically.
directions.title: Fractal Number Theory: Hausdorff Dimension of Prime Distributions

# Future Directions

## What is proved

`Catalog/Tropical/AperiodicMonotile/HierarchicalSpectrum.lean` develops a self-contained abstract hierarchy criterion. A translation period of a configuration descends through every local decoding. Decoding the level-`n` address forces the period to be divisible by `2^n`; divisibility at every level forces the period to vanish. Consequently, every member of a `SpectrumSystem` is aperiodic, and two members cannot share a nonzero period. The file also proves that the affine path `t ↦ (1-t,t)` is continuous, injective, and has the requested endpoints.

## Scope limitation

This is an abstract algebraic core, not a formalization of the actual hat and turtle polygons. In particular, it does not prove that geometric tilings by any interpolated polygon exist, that their local patches uniquely decode the binary hierarchy used here, or that a boundary in a geometric tile-parameter space is piecewise smooth. Those are the essential open formalization obligations before the proposed geometric spectrum claim can be certified.

## Natural next results

1. Define planar polygons, congruent copies, interiors, and locally finite edge-to-edge tilings in `ℝ²`.
2. Encode the hat and turtle by exact coordinates in a common kite grid, then define the genuine one-parameter tile family used in the literature rather than an abstract coordinate segment.
3. Formalize metatiles and substitution patches, including coverage, disjoint interiors, and exact boundary matching.
4. Prove recognizability: every legal tiling has a unique decomposition into level-1 supertiles.
5. Iterate recognizability to produce locally decoded addresses at every scale. Generalize the present one-dimensional divisibility argument to a rank-two lattice or expanding integer matrix.
6. Connect recognizability to the present `EnforcesHierarchy` interface and obtain geometric aperiodicity as a corollary.
7. Separately prove existence of a tiling for each parameter via nested supertiles and an appropriate compactness theorem.
8. Only after a precise finite-dimensional shape space and periodic region are defined, investigate whether their boundary is a piecewise-smooth curve. The current formalization provides no evidence for that boundary claim.

## Useful generalizations

The binary scale `2^n` can be replaced by powers of any integer `q > 1`. For planar substitutions, a matrix criterion should show that a period vector lying in every image `M^n ℤ²` is zero when `M` is expanding. A finite-radius sliding-block decoding would also model local recognizability more faithfully than the unrestricted state decoder in `FactorsThrough`.

# Future Directions

## 1. Baire-category classification of convergent prime rearrangements

**Conjecture.** In the pointwise topology on the infinite symmetric group, the set of permutations for which `p_{σ(n)}/p_n` converges is dense but meagre, while the subset with limit one is also dense and meagre.

The key insight is that finite-support permutations give density, whereas infinitely many independently prescribed index expansions and contractions should force oscillation on a residual set.

**Why now?** The finite-extension theorem settles the dense half and identifies the exact cylinder structure needed for a diagonal category argument.

## 2. Realization of every positive limiting ratio

**Conjecture.** For every real `c > 0`, there exists a permutation `σ` of the natural numbers such that `p_{σ(n)}/p_n → c`.

The key insight is that the prime number theorem turns this into an asymptotic matching problem with target index scale `σ(n) ∼ cn`; global bijectivity may be achieved by sparse corrections whose relative displacement tends to zero.

**Why now?** The dense limit-one core shows that finite constraints are harmless, allowing a construction to be assembled in long blocks while preserving any prescribed finite prefix.

## 3. Universal sequence criterion for dense ratio-one rearrangements

**Conjecture.** For a sequence in a topological group, finite-support permutations are dense among ratio-one rearrangements if and only if the sequence is eventually contained in the group of units.

The key insight is that the present argument uses only eventual invertibility and eventual fixation, not order, arithmetic growth, or primality.

**Why now?** The prime theorem has already separated the topological mechanism from number-theoretic input, suggesting a sharp abstract characterization across multiplicative groups and normed division algebras.

## 4. Local-displacement characterization under prime asymptotics

**Conjecture.** If a permutation satisfies `σ(n)/n → 1`, then `p_{σ(n)}/p_n → 1`; conversely, prime-ratio convergence to one forces `σ(n)/n → 1`.

The key insight is that the asymptotic equivalence `p_n ∼ n log n` should transport relative index displacement exactly to relative prime displacement, including along nonmonotone permutations.

**Why now?** This would identify the full well-behaved class by a purely combinatorial condition and clarify why adjacent swaps work while random macroscopic rearrangements do not.

## 5. Probability laws for explicit random infinite permutations

**Conjecture.** Under any regenerative random-permutation model with finite mean cycle-block length, the prime ratio converges almost surely to one; under heavy-tailed block laws of infinite mean, convergence exhibits a sharp tail-index transition.

The key insight is that finite cycles cause only local index displacement, while heavy-tailed blocks can create infinitely many macroscopic jumps.

**Why now?** The million-prime experiment disproves naive finite-uniform typicality and shows that a meaningful density question must begin by specifying a coherent infinite probability model.

directions.description: In the game Werewolf (Mafia), n players include k werewolves and n-k villagers. Each night, the werewolves eliminate one villager. Each day, the villagers vote to eliminate one player (possibly a werewolf). The villagers win if all werewolves are eliminated; the werewolves win if they equal or outnumber villagers. Conjecture: The optimal Bayesian strategy for villagers is to vote for the player with the highest posterior probability of being a werewolf, where the prior is k/n and the likelihood updates are based on the player's voting pattern and survival. More precisely, define the werewolf posterior P(W_i | evidence) using Bayes' theorem: P(W_i) = k/n (prior), P(evidence | W_i) = product of conditional probabilities of observed events given that player i is a werewolf. The optimal strategy maximizes P(villagers win) = P(correct elimination at each day round). For n=7, k=2: the villagers' win probability with optimal Bayesian play is approximately 0.36 (known from game theory). Conjecture: For general n and k, the villagers' win probability is approximately C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2 where C is a constant depending on the information structure. Test: simulate 10^6 games with n=7 to n=20 players and Bayesian villagers, measure the win probability, and fit to the conjectured formula. Impact: social deduction has an optimal Bayesian strategy, and the werewolves' advantage scales as (k/(n-k))^2.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the Bayesian villager strategy: at each day round, each villager computes P(W_i | evidence) for all players i, where evidence includes voting patterns and survival. Update rule: P(W_i | day_vote) proportional to P(day_vote | W_i) * P(W_i). Key likelihood: a werewolf votes to eliminate a villager with probability p_w (strategic) and a villager votes randomly with probability 1/(n-k) for each remaining player. P(villager votes for j | i is werewolf) = p_w * I(j is villager) / (n-k) + (1-p_w) * 1/(n-1). For n=7, k=2: compute optimal p_w by backward induction. The game tree has depth at most 5 (n-k rounds at most). Compute P(villagers win) by Monte Carlo simulation with 10^6 trials. For general n, k: the conjectured formula P(villagers win) = C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2 comes from the observation that each day round eliminates a werewolf with probability k/(n-1) * (1 + information_advantage), so the expected number of werewolves eliminated before all villagers die is (n-k) * k/(n-1) * C'. Simplify to get C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2. Test: verify for n=7 to n=20.
directions.title: Bayesian Werewolf: Optimal Strategy for Social Deduction Games

directions.description: A dataset with missing values is a sheaf on a poset: the poset is the set of feature subsets (ordered by inclusion), and the sheaf assigns to each feature subset the set of complete observations on those features. The missing data creates 'holes' in the sheaf: H^0 measures the global sections (complete observations) and H^1 measures the obstructions to patching local observations into global ones. Conjecture: For a dataset with missing rate r, the dimension of H^1 is approximately r * n * (r * log(1/r)), where n is the number of features. This means: the 'amount of missing information' grows super-linearly with the missing rate, and imputation is fundamentally harder than interpolation because H^1 > 0 means there is no consistent way to fill in the missing data. The sheaf-theoretic imputation: fill in missing values by finding the section s in H^0 that minimizes the coboundary delta(s) in H^1. This is the maximum likelihood imputation under the assumption that the data is locally consistent. Test: generate synthetic datasets with known ground truth, introduce missing values at rate r, compute H^0 and H^1 of the data sheaf, and verify dim(H^1) ~ r*n*r*log(1/r). Compare sheaf-theoretic imputation with standard methods (mean, KNN, MICE). Impact: missing data is a topological problem, and the sheaf cohomology tells you exactly how much information is lost and whether it can be recovered.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the data sheaf: for a dataset with n features and m observations, the poset P is the set of feature subsets S subset {1,...,n} ordered by inclusion. The sheaf F assigns to each S the set of observations that have all features in S present (complete rows restricted to columns in S). The restriction maps F(S) -> F(T) for T subset S are projections that drop columns in S\T. Define H^0(F) = ker(delta_0) = global sections (observations complete on ALL features). Define H^1(F) = ker(delta_1)/im(delta_0) = obstructions to patching local observations into global ones. Compute delta_0 and delta_1 using the Cech complex. Estimate dim(H^1): for missing rate r and n features, each observation is missing r*n features on average. The expected number of complete observations is m*(1-r)^n (each feature present with probability 1-r). The obstruction dim(H^1) grows with the number of incompatible local patches. Each missing feature creates a potential obstruction. Estimated dim(H^1) ~ m * r * (1-(1-r)^n) ~ m * r * n * r for small r. Test: generate data from a known multivariate normal, introduce MCAR missing values at rate r, compute H^0 and H^1, fit dim(H^1) ~ C * r * n * r * log(1/r).
directions.title: Sheaf Cohomology of Data: The Topology of Missing Information

# Future Directions: Complex-Weighted Random Graph Spectra

## 1. Directed fixed-amplitude circular law
Let each ordered off-diagonal edge be present independently with probability `p`, give every present edge amplitude `z`, subtract the mean matrix, and normalize by `|z|√(np(1-p))`. Conjecture: for fixed `0 < p < 1` and nonzero `z`, the empirical spectral distribution converges to the uniform measure on the unit disk.

The key insight is that directing the edges removes the transpose correlation that forces undirected spectra onto a line, while centering removes the rank-one mean outlier.

Why now? The exact phase-locking obstruction identifies both modifications—direction and centering—that the original model lacked, making this a sharply specified replacement rather than a cosmetic variant.

## 2. Sparse directed threshold for circular behavior
For directed edges with `pₙ → 0`, conjecture that the centered, variance-normalized empirical spectrum obeys the circular law whenever `npₙ` grows faster than a logarithmic threshold, while below that scale isolated rows create a nonvanishing atom at zero.

The key insight is that the same sparsity scale controlling isolated vertices also controls singularity and hence the failure of two-dimensional spectral spreading.

Why now? The finite product-law infrastructure already separates exact edge independence from asymptotic analysis, and the deterministic obstruction shows that sparsity must be studied only after the symmetry issue is repaired.

## 3. Independently phased undirected edges
Assign each undirected edge an independent unit-modulus phase and place conjugate weights across the diagonal, producing a Hermitian magnetic adjacency matrix. Conjecture: after centering and variance normalization, the empirical spectrum converges to the semicircle law, independent of the phase distribution provided its first two moments are nondegenerate.

The key insight is that conjugate transpose symmetry, not the mere presence of complex phases, determines the one-dimensional limiting geometry.

Why now? Exact adjoint calculations for constant phase expose the invariant that survives randomization and predict semicircular rather than circular behavior for magnetic undirected graphs.

## 4. Rank-one outlier transition
For dense directed complex-weighted Bernoulli matrices without centering, conjecture that one eigenvalue lies asymptotically near `zpn`, while all remaining eigenvalues have scale `|z|√(np(1-p))`; after centering, the outlier disappears.

The key insight is that the entry mean contributes a rank-one deterministic matrix whose eigenvalue is linear in `n`, whereas fluctuations are only of square-root order.

Why now? The explicit four-vertex complete-graph witness already demonstrates the linear-scale mean direction and gives a finite deterministic prototype of the asymptotic outlier.

## 5. Quantitative pseudospectral separation
For the directed centered model, conjecture a high-probability lower bound on the least singular value of `A-wI`, uniform for `w` outside a slightly enlarged circular-law disk, with constants depending explicitly on `p` and `|z|`.

The key insight is that eigenvalue plots alone cannot distinguish genuine circular behavior from nonnormal pseudospectral instability; least-singular-value control supplies the missing robust criterion.

Why now? The undirected model is exactly normal, so replacing it by a directed model introduces nonnormality as a new phenomenon that must be quantified rather than inferred visually.

directions.description: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle states that Delta(x) * Delta(p) >= hbar/2. But this is NOT a physical principle — it is a THEOREM of Fourier analysis. The Fourier transform of a function f(x) satisfies: if f is concentrated in a region of width Delta(x), then its Fourier transform f_hat is concentrated in a region of width Delta(k) >= 1/(2*Delta(x)). This is the Benedicks-Amrein-Berthier theorem: a function and its Fourier transform cannot both be supported on sets of finite measure. Conjecture: The uncertainty principle generalizes to all integral transforms. For the Laplace transform: if f is supported on [a, infinity), then the Laplace transform L[f](s) cannot be supported on a set of finite measure unless f = 0. For the Mellin transform: if f is supported on a geometric progression, then M[f](s) cannot be supported on a set of finite measure. For the Radon transform: if f is supported on a strip, then R[f] cannot be supported on a set of finite measure. The general principle: no invertible integral transform allows both a function and its transform to have compact support. Test: verify the uncertainty principle for the Fourier, Laplace, Mellin, and Radon transforms numerically. Construct functions with Delta(x) = epsilon and measure Delta(k) for each transform. Impact: the uncertainty principle is not about quantum mechanics — it is about the structure of integral transforms. Every transform has its own uncertainty principle.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Fourier uncertainty principle: for f in L^2(R), ||x*f||_2 * ||k*f_hat||_2 >= ||f||_2^2/2. Equality iff f is a Gaussian. Prove the Benedicks theorem: if f is supported on a set of finite measure and f_hat is also supported on a set of finite measure, then f = 0. Generalize to the Laplace transform: if f is supported on [a, infinity) and L[f](s) = integral f(t) e^{-st} dt is supported on a set of finite measure in s, then f = 0. Proof: L[f](s) is analytic in Re(s) > 0 (since f is supported on [0, infinity)), and an analytic function that vanishes on a set of positive measure vanishes identically. Generalize to Mellin: if f is supported on a geometric progression {a*r^n : n in Z} and M[f](s) = integral f(t) t^{s-1} dt has support of finite measure, then f = 0. Generalize to Radon: if f is supported on a strip |x_1| < a and R[f](theta, s) has support of finite measure in (theta, s), then f = 0. Test: numerically construct functions with Delta(x) = epsilon and measure Delta(k) for each transform. Verify Delta(x) * Delta(k) >= C for transform-specific constant C.
directions.title: The Uncertainty Principle Is a Fourier Thing: Position-Momentum Duality

# Future Directions: Alexander Spectra of Knotted Light

## 1. Composite torus knots split into cyclotomic spectral strata

**Conjecture.** For every odd positive integer `n`, the angular spectrum selected by the `T(2,n)` Alexander polynomial is the disjoint union of primitive `2d`-th root strata over all divisors `d > 1` of `n`. The multiplicity-free channel count is therefore the sum of `φ(2d)` over those divisors.

The key insight is that the alternating Alexander polynomial satisfies `(X+1)A_n(X)=X^n+1`, whose cyclotomic factors are indexed by the divisors of `n`.

**Why now?** The prime case has been reduced exactly to coprimality modulo `2p`; composite parameters are the next falsifiable test of whether spectral splitting tracks arithmetic factorization.

## 2. Optical products realize convolution in modular unit groups

**Conjecture.** Under multiplication of two prime torus-knot phase filters with moduli `2p` and `2q`, the resulting angular channels are governed by the image of `(ℤ/2pℤ)ˣ × (ℤ/2qℤ)ˣ` under the Chinese remainder correspondence, with degeneracies determined by `gcd(p,q)`.

The key insight is that each prime torus spectrum is not merely a set of roots but a torsor for a modular unit group, while optical phase multiplication adds angular indices.

**Why now?** Exact coprimality selection and charge additivity are both available, making their interaction a concrete algebraic prediction rather than a qualitative analogy.

## 3. Off-circle Alexander roots predict evanescent rather than OAM channels

**Conjecture.** For reciprocal Alexander polynomials with no unit-circle roots, each reciprocal pair `r, r⁻¹` controls a pair of exponentially growing and decaying radial modes, not real angular OAM residues. For the figure-eight knot, the rates are the logarithms of `(3 ± √5)/2`.

The key insight is that angular propagation detects root argument, whereas radial growth detects root modulus; reducing a real root modulo one confuses these two observables.

**Why now?** The figure-eight polynomial has been proved to vanish nowhere on every angular grid, sharply isolating the alternative physical interpretation that must be tested.

## 4. Mahler measure bounds spectral radial instability

**Conjecture.** For a knotted optical field whose transfer polynomial is the Alexander polynomial, the total radial Lyapunov growth equals the logarithmic Mahler measure of that polynomial. Cyclotomic torus knots have zero growth, while the figure-eight knot has positive growth `2 log φ`.

The key insight is that Mahler measure sums the logarithmic moduli of roots outside the unit circle, exactly the data discarded by a root-of-unity-only spectrum.

**Why now?** The established cyclotomic/off-circle dichotomy supplies explicit zero-growth and positive-growth test cases with reciprocal root geometry.

## 5. Spectral measurements recover torus-knot parameters

**Conjecture.** Within the family `T(2,p)` for odd primes, the number of distinct Alexander-selected angular channels and their modular addition table uniquely determine `p`, and hence determine the Alexander polynomial and knot determinant.

The key insight is that the channel set is the full unit group modulo `2p`, has cardinality `p−1`, and is a single cyclotomic Galois orbit.

**Why now?** The exact residue classification turns an inverse optical problem into a finite reconstruction problem with an immediately testable uniqueness criterion.

# Future Directions: Jigsaw Complexity and Topology

## 1. Geometric NP-completeness with four-sided pieces

Conjecture: deciding whether a finite multiset of non-rotatable square pieces with flat, tab, and blank edges tiles a prescribed rectangle is NP-complete, even when each non-flat edge carries one of only finitely many colors and every valid tiling has a fixed outer frame.

The key insight is that the assignment-level bijection should survive replacement of the abstract clause predicate by planar wire, crossover, fan-out, and clause gadgets whose unused interfaces are forced by the frame.

Why now? The exact witness correspondence isolates the sole missing burden: a polynomial-size geometric realization that introduces neither spurious assemblies nor lost satisfying assignments.

## 2. Parsimonious counting hardness

Conjecture: there is a geometric gadget family for which the number of rectangular assemblies equals the number of satisfying assignments, up to a formula-independent symmetry factor computable in polynomial time.

The key insight is that witness preservation is stronger than equisatisfiability and naturally targets counting reductions; rigid framing should quotient out translations, rotations, and interchangeable copies.

Why now? The abstract construction already gives a canonical bijection of witness spaces, so every discrepancy in a geometric implementation can be localized to gadget automorphisms.

## 3. Complementation as a free involution

Conjecture: for every framed puzzle not isomorphic to its global tab–blank complement, complementation acts freely on the disjoint union of the two assembly spaces, forcing their combined cardinality to be even.

The key insight is that simultaneous Boolean negation and literal-polarity reversal is an order-two transport of complete solution spaces, not merely a preservation of solvability.

Why now? Solvability invariance has been established, while the exact boundary between free orbits and self-dual fixed configurations is now explicit and testable.

## 4. Homology-valued boundary obstruction

Conjecture: for puzzles assembled on an orientable surface, signed edge potentials define a cohomology class whose pairing with every noncontractible cycle must vanish; on a rectangle this reduces to tab–blank conservation, while on a torus it gives two independent flux obstructions.

The key insight is that local complementary cancellation is a discrete divergence law, and nontrivial first homology records flux that cannot be removed by pairing interior edges.

Why now? Existing strip and grid conservation laws provide the contractible base cases from which cycle decompositions and surface gluings can be developed.

## 5. Topology of the solution complex

Conjecture: there are parsimonious jigsaw gadgets for which the cubical complex generated by single-variable flips deformation-retracts onto the corresponding SAT solution complex.

The key insight is that preserving witnesses alone captures vertices, whereas controlled local reconfiguration can preserve adjacency, connected components, and ultimately homotopy type.

Why now? A canonical vertex bijection is available; the next falsifiable step is to characterize exactly when one-variable changes correspond to bounded local rearrangements of pieces.

directions.description: The chromatic polynomial chi_G(k) counts the number of proper k-colorings of a graph G. For a friendship graph, chi_G(k) counts the number of ways to assign k emotions to people such that no two friends share the same emotion. Conjecture: The chromatic polynomial evaluated at k=6 (for the 6 basic emotions: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise) gives the number of 'emotionally consistent' assignments of emotions to a social network. The chromatic polynomial has a root at k=2 for any bipartite graph, meaning a social network that splits cleanly into two groups has exactly 0 ways to assign 2 emotions without friends sharing emotions. The real emotional chromatic number chi_E(G) of a social network G is the smallest k such that chi_G(k) > 0 and k >= 3 (since real emotions need at least 3 categories to avoid trivial assignments). For a complete graph K_n (a clique of n mutual friends), chi_E(K_n) = n (everyone needs a different emotion). For a cycle C_n (a circular friendship chain), chi_E(C_n) = 2 if n is even and 3 if n is odd (alternating emotions work for even cycles, but odd cycles need a third emotion). Test: compute chi_E(G) for 100 real social networks and verify that the emotional chromatic number is between 3 and 6 for most networks. Impact: the chromatic polynomial is not just combinatorics — it measures the emotional diversity of a social network.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the emotional chromatic number chi_E(G) = min{k >= 3 : chi_G(k) > 0}. For a graph G with n vertices and m edges, compute chi_G(k) using the deletion-contraction recurrence: chi_G(k) = chi_{G-e}(k) - chi_{G/e}(k). For social networks: the emotional chromatic number is the minimum number of emotions needed to ensure no two friends share the same emotion. For a complete graph K_n: chi_E = n (every person needs a different emotion). For a cycle C_n: chi_E = 2 if n even, 3 if n odd (but chi_E >= 3, so for even cycles chi_E = 3 by the minimum constraint). For a path P_n: chi_E = 3 (alternating two emotions doesn't satisfy k >= 3). For random graphs G(n, p): chi_E is approximately max(3, n / (2*log(n/p))) by the chromatic number asymptotics. Test: compute chi_E for 100 social networks from SNAP or similar databases. Verify: most social networks have chi_E between 3 and 6. The 6 basic emotions (Ekman) provide a natural upper bound.
directions.title: Graph Coloring with Emotions: The Chromatic Polynomial Meets Psychology

# Future Directions: Geometry Beyond Integer Linking

## 1. A real-valued Hopf-geometric concurrence functional

There exists a canonically normalized real-valued functional on the quaternionic Hopf geometry of a two-qubit state that is continuous, vanishes exactly on product states, and equals one exactly on maximally entangled states.

**The key insight is...** ordinary linking numbers are too discrete, but differential-geometric quantities such as calibrated volume, holonomy, or an averaged linking integral can vary continuously with the determinant coordinate.

**Why now?** The integer-valued proposal is obstructed by an explicit normalized state of concurrence one half, sharply specifying the properties a replacement invariant must satisfy.

## 2. Exterior-algebra characterization of multipartite entanglement

For each bipartition of a pure multipartite state, the complete family of Plücker coordinates of the corresponding coefficient flattening determines a hierarchy of entanglement monotones, with the two-qubit concurrence as its first nontrivial member.

**The key insight is...** two-qubit concurrence is the norm of a determinant, and determinants are the coordinates of exterior powers rather than linking numbers.

**Why now?** The determinant bound and its exact zero locus provide a tractable base case from which higher minors and their norm inequalities can be developed.

## 3. Classification of all sharp determinant maximizers

Every normalized two-qubit state with concurrence one lies in the local-unitary orbit of a Bell state, and equality in the determinant norm bound is equivalent to orthogonality and equal norm of the two coefficient rows.

**The key insight is...** equality must hold simultaneously in the triangle inequality and both quadratic product bounds, forcing rigid phase and norm relations.

**Why now?** The sharp upper bound is established, and its proof exposes the exact inequalities whose equality cases must be classified.

## 4. Quantitative distance from the product-state variety

There are optimal universal constants relating concurrence to the metric distance from a normalized state to the Segre variety of product states, for both Euclidean and Fubini–Study metrics.

**The key insight is...** concurrence is the norm of the defining quadratic equation of the Segre variety, so it should control transverse distance while degenerating predictably along tangent directions.

**Why now?** The exact determinant criterion identifies the algebraic zero set, while the unit-interval bound supplies the global normalization needed for sharp estimates.

## 5. Topological stratification of fixed-concurrence level sets

For each `c` strictly between zero and one, the normalized two-qubit states of concurrence `c`, modulo global phase, have a uniform diffeomorphism type, with topology changing only at the product and maximally entangled strata.

**The key insight is...** although concurrence itself cannot be an integer linking number, its critical level sets may still carry meaningful and computable topology.

**Why now?** Explicit interior values and the two boundary values are available, making the conjecture falsifiable through a combination of singular-value coordinates and level-set analysis.

directions.description: In 1952, Turing showed that reaction-diffusion equations produce patterns (spots, stripes, spirals) that explain biological morphogenesis. But Turing patterns are solutions to PDEs, which are hard to analyze. Conjecture: Turing patterns are algebraic varieties. Specifically, the zero set of a Turing pattern (where the concentration equals the background level) is a real algebraic curve in 2D (for spots and stripes) or a real algebraic surface in 3D (for more complex patterns). The degree of the curve is the number of modes in the reaction-diffusion system. For a two-mode system (like the Gray-Scott model), the pattern is a curve of degree 2 (a conic section: circles for spots, parallel lines for stripes, hyperbolas for labyrinthine patterns). For a three-mode system, the pattern is a curve of degree up to 6 (sextic curves that can produce hexagonal patterns). The genus of the curve determines the pattern topology: genus 0 gives spots (topologically a sphere), genus 1 gives stripes (topologically a torus), and genus g > 1 gives labyrinthine patterns with g+1 holes. Test: simulate Turing patterns in the Gray-Scott model, fit the zero-set to an algebraic curve of degree d, and verify that d = 2 for spots and stripes. Compute the genus and verify it matches the pattern topology. Impact: biological patterns are algebraic curves. The mathematics of seashells, leopard spots, and zebra stripes is the mathematics of conic sections.
directions.proof_strategy: The Turing pattern u(x,y) satisfies the reaction-diffusion equation: partial_t u = D * nabla^2 u + f(u, v), partial_t v = D' * nabla^2 v + g(u, v). At steady state: D * nabla^2 u + f(u, v) = 0. The zero set {u = u_0} (where u_0 is the background concentration) is the pattern boundary. Linearize around the uniform state: u = u_0 + epsilon * w(x,y) where w satisfies D * nabla^2 w + f_u * w + f_v * z = 0 and similarly for z. The eigenfunctions are e^{i*k*x} with k determined by the Turing conditions. For a two-mode system, w = A*cos(k1*x) + B*cos(k2*y), so the zero set is A*cos(k1*x) + B*cos(k2*y) = u_0, which is approximately a degree-2 algebraic curve (ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola depending on k1, k2). For spots: A = B, k1 = k2 gives circles (degree 2). For stripes: A >> B gives parallel lines (degree 2 degenerate). For hexagonal patterns: three modes with k1, k2, k3 at 60 degrees give a degree-6 curve. Compute: fit the zero set of a simulated Turing pattern to an algebraic curve using least-squares polynomial regression. Verify the degree matches the number of modes. Test: Gray-Scott model with parameters for spots (F=0.035, k=0.065), stripes (F=0.025, k=0.055), labyrinthine (F=0.02, k=0.05).
directions.title: Turing's Flowers: Morphogenesis as Algebraic Geometry

The formalization establishes the foundational deletion-stability theory for complete sets:
strong completeness is equivalent to completeness of every tail (and even of all sufficiently
late tails), is invariant under finite symmetric difference, and admits an equivalent
cofinite-subset formulation.

The next major target is the paper's analytic criterion. A faithful route would require:

1. Formalize the distance to the nearest integer `‖x‖` and the divergence condition
   `∑ a ∈ A, ‖a * θ‖ = ∞` as a statement about filters or infinite sums of nonnegative terms.
2. Define ordered blocks and prove the general block criterion from which the dyadic theorem
   follows. This should separate the combinatorial subset-sum argument from the Fourier or
   equidistribution input.
3. Develop the finite block lemmas controlling subset sums when each sufficiently late dyadic
   block contains at least six elements.
4. Connect the analytic divergence hypothesis to the combinatorial hypotheses needed for
   completeness of every tail. The theorem `stronglyComplete_iff_eventually_complete_tails`
   then turns this into strong completeness directly.
5. Instantiate the block criterion with `(2^k, 2^(k+1)]` and formalize the stated resolution of
   Erdős's conjecture.

A smaller next step is to prove concrete complete-set examples (binary powers and suitable
finite unions of lacunary sequences), then test which remain complete after deletions. This
would exercise the definitions before undertaking the paper's analytic core.

# Future directions

1. **Heterogeneous planets.** Generalize the equal-rate formula `(1-p)^N` to `∏ i, (1-pᵢ)` and prove `1 - ∏ i, (1-pᵢ) ≤ ∑ i, pᵢ` over finite populations.
2. **Dependence without independence.** Formalize a finite probability space and prove the union bound directly for arbitrary civilization events. The present product formula specifically encodes independence, while Markov’s inequality only needs a nonnegative count.
3. **Random counts.** Prove `Pr[X ≥ 1] ≤ E[X]` for natural-valued random variables and derive the emptiness lower bound as a complement. This would make precise which conclusion follows solely from expectation.
4. **Uncertain Drake factors.** Treat each filter as an interval or random variable, deriving robust upper bounds for expected count rather than fixing disputed numerical estimates.
5. **Time windows and observability.** Add birth times, lifetime intervals, signal travel, and detection events. Distinguish “no civilization exists,” “none overlaps our era,” and “no detectable contact occurs.”
6. **Sharper independent bounds.** Compare the exact value `(1-p)^N` with exponential estimates such as `(1-p)^N ≤ exp(-Np)` and quantify when the first-order union bound is informative.
7. **Sparse occupancy structure.** Strengthen `many_planets_empty` to exact identities for occupied and empty planets and characterize equality in terms of injectivity of the home-planet map.
8. **Empirical separation.** Keep astronomical assumptions outside the mathematical theorem: observational estimates of candidate counts and biological filter probabilities require data and cannot be established by pigeonhole arguments alone.

The formal results do not establish that humanity is alone. They establish conditional probability bounds for an explicit model and formally refute the stronger inference from expectation below one to certainty of emptiness.

# Future Directions

## 1. Entropy dimension for genuinely submultiplicative search languages

**Conjecture.** Let `N(n)` be the number of successful prefixes of length `n` in a finitely branching search language, and suppose `N(n+m) ≤ N(n)N(m)` with `N(n) ≥ 1`. Then the normalized logarithmic growth rate exists and equals the infimum of the finite-scale rates. Under a compatible ultrametric and a finite-type extension condition, this rate also equals the Hausdorff dimension of the infinite successful-path boundary.

The key insight is that the exact additivity proved for finite profiles should be replaced by subadditivity, while the relative-entropy normalization remains unchanged. **Why now?** The finite multiscale composition law identifies precisely which quantity must survive when exact self-similarity is weakened.

## 2. Ergodic branching and almost-sure dimension

**Conjecture.** For a stationary ergodic sequence of ambient and successful branching pairs `(Bₙ,Sₙ)` satisfying `1 ≤ Sₙ ≤ Bₙ` and suitable logarithmic integrability, the almost-sure proof-search dimension is

`E[log S₀] / E[log B₀]`.

The key insight is that logarithmic path volumes are additive cocycles, so their ratio should converge by ergodic averaging. **Why now?** The deterministic profile theorem supplies the exact finite-block identity whose random-block limit this conjecture predicts.

## 3. Dimension spectrum under finite-state pruning

**Conjecture.** For successful paths accepted by a strongly connected finite-state pruning automaton over a fixed `b`-ary tree, the dimension equals `log ρ(A) / log b`, where `ρ(A)` is the spectral radius of the automaton's nonnegative transition matrix. Moreover, every algebraic number arising as such a normalized Perron root is realizable by a finite-state proof-search geometry.

The key insight is that scalar products of branching numbers generalize to matrix products, with Perron growth replacing ordinary multiplication. **Why now?** The nonstationary scalar theory clarifies the exact point at which linear algebra should enter and provides the expected normalization.

## 4. Policy-sensitive search cost at fixed dimension

**Conjecture.** For every rational `d` strictly between zero and one and every computable unbounded function `f`, there are two finitely branching search instances with the same successful-prefix dimension `d` but deterministic depth-first discovery costs whose ratio exceeds `f(n)` at infinitely many depths.

The key insight is that dimension measures abundance, whereas a search policy measures ordering; adversarial rearrangement can preserve all prefix counts while moving successful terminals arbitrarily late. **Why now?** The current entropy laws sharply characterize geometry, making it possible to isolate and test the independent contribution of traversal policy.

## 5. Stability under sparse adversarial perturbations

**Conjecture.** If two nonstationary branching profiles differ on a set of levels of asymptotic density zero and their branching numbers are uniformly bounded above and below away from the unary degeneration, then their limiting relative entropy dimensions agree whenever either limit exists.

The key insight is that sparse changes contribute sublinear error to both logarithmic volumes. **Why now?** Repetition invariance and weighted composition already establish the finite-block algebra needed to quantify the effect of exceptional blocks.

directions.description: The Riemann zeta function zeta(s) has zeros at the non-trivial points s = 1/2 + i*gamma_n where gamma_n are the imaginary parts of the zeros. The Fourier transform of the zero counting function N(t) = #{gamma_n <= t} is related to the distribution of primes by the explicit formula. But what if we take the Fourier transform of zeta itself? Define Z(t) = zeta(1/2 + it) as a function of the real variable t. The Fourier transform Z_hat(w) = integral_{-inf}^{inf} Z(t) * e^{-2*pi*i*w*t} dt. Conjecture: Z_hat(w) has sharp peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi for each prime p. This is because the explicit formula expresses zeta(1/2+it) as a sum over primes: zeta(1/2+it) ~ sum_{p} p^{-1/2-it} = sum_{p} e^{-it*log(p)} / sqrt(p), which is a sum of complex exponentials with frequencies log(p). The Fourier transform of a sum of exponentials is a sum of delta functions at the frequencies log(p)/2*pi. So Z_hat(w) = sum_{p} delta(w - log(p)/2*pi) / sqrt(p) + (error from zeros and smooth terms). The peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi give a 'spectrogram' of the primes. Test: compute Z_hat(w) numerically for the first 10^6 zeros and verify the peaks at log(2)/2*pi, log(3)/2*pi, log(5)/2*pi, etc. Impact: you can HEAR the primes by playing the Fourier transform of the Riemann zeta function — each prime is a distinct note.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Z(t) = zeta(1/2 + it) for real t. The Fourier transform Z_hat(w) = integral Z(t) e^{-2*pi*i*w*t} dt. By the explicit formula: zeta(1/2+it) = sum_{p} p^{-1/2-it} + (terms from zeros and smooth parts). The prime sum = sum_p e^{-it*log(p)} / sqrt(p). Fourier transform of e^{-it*log(p)} is delta(w - log(p)/2*pi). So Z_hat(w) = sum_p delta(w - log(p)/2*pi) / sqrt(p) + (smooth error). The error terms come from: (1) the trivial zeros at s = -2n, contributing e^{-2*pi*i*w*2n} = delta(w = n), (2) the non-trivial zeros, contributing a smooth background, (3) the logarithmic derivative of the gamma factor. The key insight: the peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi are SHARP (delta-function-like) because there are infinitely many zeros that reinforce these frequencies. Compute numerically: evaluate Z(t) for t in [0, T] with step dt, compute FFT, and look for peaks at w = log(2)/2*pi ≈ 0.110, log(3)/2*pi ≈ 0.174, log(5)/2*pi ≈ 0.256, etc. Test: verify peaks at these frequencies using the first 10^6 zeros with T = 10^6.
directions.title: The Fourier Transform of the Riemann Zeta: Hearing the Primes

directions.description: The sequence of primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ... defines a point cloud in R where the n-th prime p_n is at position p_n on the real line. The gaps between primes create a topological structure. Define the persistent homology of the prime point cloud as the Rips filtration R_epsilon = {p_n : |p_m - p_n| <= epsilon}. As epsilon increases, more primes are connected, and the topology changes. Conjecture: The persistent H_0 (connected components) of the prime point cloud has the same barcode as a Poisson point process with intensity 1/log(x). Specifically, the bar lengths in H_0 follow an exponential distribution with mean equal to the average prime gap (which is approximately log(x) by the prime number theorem). The persistent H_1 (1-dimensional holes) of the prime point cloud appears at scale epsilon ~ log(x)^2, corresponding to prime pairs (p, p+2k) where 2k is a specific even gap. The longest H_1 bar corresponds to the twin prime conjecture: it persists from epsilon = 2 (the twin prime scale) to epsilon = infinity. Test: compute persistent homology of the primes up to 10^6 using Rips filtration and compare with the Poisson point process prediction. Verify that H_0 bar lengths are exponentially distributed with mean log(x). Impact: primes have topology — their gaps create persistent homology that encodes the twin prime conjecture and other arithmetic properties.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the prime point cloud P_N = {p_1, p_2, ..., p_N} subset R. The Rips complex R_epsilon(P_N) connects p_i and p_j if |p_i - p_j| <= epsilon. H_0: at epsilon = 0, each prime is its own component. At epsilon = 2, twin primes are connected (p, p+2). At epsilon = 4, cousin primes are connected. At epsilon = log(x), most nearby primes are connected. The bar lengths in H_0 are the prime gaps: bar i has length g_i = p_{i+1} - p_i. By Cramer's model, the prime gaps follow an approximate exponential distribution: P(g = 2k) ~ 2*C_2 * k^{-2} * (1/log(p))^1 for even k (and 0 for odd k > 1). This is NOT an exponential distribution — it is a power law with a correction. The Poisson prediction P(g > epsilon) ~ e^{-epsilon/log(x)} overestimates long gaps. Correct: the H_0 bar lengths follow the prime gap distribution, which is approximately geometric with parameter 1/log(p). H_1: 1-dimensional holes appear when three primes p_a, p_b, p_c form a triangle with all gaps <= epsilon. This happens at epsilon = max(p_b - p_a, p_c - p_b, p_c - p_a). The H_1 bars encode constellations of 3+ primes in a short interval. Test: compute persistent homology of primes up to 10^6 using GUDHI or Ripser, extract H_0 and H_1 barcodes, compare with Poisson model.

directions.description: The logistic map f(x) = r*x*(1-x) for r = 4 exhibits chaotic dynamics: small changes in initial conditions lead to exponentially diverging trajectories (Lyapunov exponent lambda = log(2)). This sensitivity to initial conditions is exactly what a cryptosystem needs. Conjecture: The logistic map at r = 4 is a secure pseudorandom generator. Define the logistic cipher: key = (x_0, n) where x_0 in (0,1) is the seed and n is the number of iterations. The keystream is K = (f^n(x_0), f^{n+1}(x_0), ...) where f^n denotes the n-th iterate. The ciphertext is C = M XOR K where M is the plaintext. The security relies on two properties: (1) Sensitivity: a change of epsilon in x_0 leads to a change of O(1) in f^n(x_0) after n = O(log(1/epsilon)) iterations (exponential sensitivity). (2) Ergodicity: the distribution of f^n(x_0) converges to the invariant measure mu(x) = 1/(pi*sqrt(x*(1-x))) regardless of the initial condition. Conjecture: breaking the logistic cipher (recovering x_0 from K) is as hard as inverting the logistic map, which requires solving a degree-2^n polynomial (since f^n(x) is a polynomial of degree 2^n). This is exponential in n. Test: implement the logistic cipher, measure the period of the keystream (which should be at least 2^n for floating-point precision n), and verify that statistical tests (NIST SP 800-22) pass for n >= 64. Impact: chaos IS cryptography — the logistic map's sensitivity to initial conditions is the same property that makes encryption secure.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the logistic cipher: key = (x_0, n) where x_0 in (0,1), n >= 1. Keystream: K_i = floor(256 * f^{n+i}(x_0)) for i = 0, 1, 2, .... Ciphertext: C_i = M_i XOR K_i. Decryption: compute K from (x_0, n) and XOR again. Security analysis: (1) f^n(x) is a polynomial of degree 2^n in x. Solving f^n(x) = y for x requires finding the roots of a degree-2^n polynomial, which takes O(2^n) time. (2) The Lyapunov exponent lambda = log(2) means that an epsilon error in x_0 propagates to an O(1) error after O(log(1/epsilon)) iterations. For double precision (epsilon = 2^{-52}), this takes about 52 iterations. (3) The invariant measure is the arcsine distribution: mu(x) = 1/(pi*sqrt(x*(1-x))). Keystream bits are approximately uniform. (4) Period: in double precision, the logistic map has a period of at most 2^{52} (due to floating-point representation). In exact arithmetic, the period is infinite. Attack model: given K_0, K_1, ..., K_m, find x_0. This requires solving f^n(x_0) = y_0 where y_0 = K_0/256, which is a degree-2^n polynomial. Test: implement in Python, run NIST SP 800-22 tests for n = 64, 128, 256.
directions.title: Cryptography from Chaos: Encrypting with the Logistic Map

# Future Directions

1. **Variable branching alphabets.** Generalize binary profiles to a fixed `b`-ary alphabet and prove that normalization by `log b` again bounds dimension by `1` and realizes rational free-level densities.

2. **Aperiodic pruning.** Replace periodic residue sets by arbitrary sets of free levels. Relate upper box dimension to the limsup of free-level densities and lower box dimension to the corresponding liminf.

3. **Search policy and cost.** Enrich `SearchInstance` with an exploration order, failed-branch costs, and terminal nodes. The present non-determination theorem shows that these semantic data are necessary before dimension can imply proof-search time or shortest-proof length.

4. **Finite-sample bounds.** Extend the exact complete-period result to explicit error bounds at arbitrary depths. The existing free-count sandwich suggests an error of order `R.card / n`.

5. **Entropy formulation.** Express dimension as normalized entropy growth for nonuniform profiles and investigate subadditive hypotheses under which the limiting entropy exists.

6. **Monotonicity under pruning.** Develop operations on search profiles (intersection, union, and levelwise restriction) and prove corresponding dimension inequalities, allowing modular comparison of proof-search strategies.

# Future Directions

## 1. Adaptive-submodularity criterion for greedy posterior voting

**Conjecture.** In a finite social-deduction game whose information states form a belief-state Markov process, maximum-posterior elimination is globally optimal whenever the village continuation value is adaptively submodular in the set of eliminated wolves and exchangeable under permutations of surviving identities.

The key insight is that the proved affine continuation theorem is the one-step, modular boundary case of a broader diminishing-returns principle. **Why now?** The exact boundary between local classification optimality and sequential optimality has been isolated, making exchangeability and diminishing returns separately testable.

## 2. Value-of-information phase transition

**Conjecture.** For fixed wolf density below one half, there is a critical signal-to-noise ratio in an exchangeable voting-channel model above which Bayesian villagers have win probability bounded away from zero uniformly in population size, while below it their win probability converges to the information-free baseline.

The key insight is that posterior concentration, rather than posterior ranking alone, should control whether information overcomes the wolves' elimination rate. **Why now?** The exact information-free recurrence supplies a null model, and likelihood channels can be compared against it through posterior concentration inequalities.

## 3. Parity-corrected asymptotics for the information-free game

**Conjecture.** For every fixed wolf count `k`, the information-free village win probabilities have two distinct asymptotic expansions according to the parity of the initial population, with a common leading limit but different first-order corrections.

The key insight is that daytime and nighttime villager losses occur in pairs after a miss, preserving a parity trace until absorption. **Why now?** Exact values from seven through twenty players show a stable even/odd oscillation that the proposed single quadratic scaling cannot capture.

## 4. Spin-system representation of correlated suspicion

**Conjecture.** Under a pairwise log-linear likelihood model for voting histories, the posterior over role assignments is an Ising model conditioned on fixed total wolf number; Bayesian role complementation acts as spin flip, while vote correlations become couplings whose sign predicts coalition polarization.

The key insight is that the centered one-player posterior already transforms exactly as an Ising spin, and pairwise log likelihoods naturally become quadratic spin interactions. **Why now?** The one-site symmetry bridge is established, so the next falsifiable step is to derive and test the full constrained Gibbs representation.

## 5. Sequential regret for approximate posterior voting

**Conjecture.** In identity-symmetric continuation models under calibrated Bayesian updates, the cumulative regret of approximate posterior voting admits a horizon-sensitive martingale bound in terms of the successive posterior approximation errors.

The key insight is that the exact one-step theorem bounds regret by `(good-bad)ε`, turning posterior approximation error directly into utility regret. **Why now?** The one-step coefficient and its sharp linear dependence are established, leaving the concrete problem of controlling how these errors propagate through sequential belief updates.

directions.description: Category theory studies objects and morphisms between them. A joke has a setup (an object) and a punchline (a morphism that subverts expectations). Define the category Joke where objects are setups and morphisms are punchlines. A joke J: S -> P is a morphism from setup S to punchline P that factors through an unexpected category. The humor of a joke is measured by its 'surprise': the distance between the expected punchline (the limit of the setup category) and the actual punchline. Conjecture: The funniest jokes are those where the setup category has a colimit that is far from the limit. Formally, if S is a setup with expected resolution lim(S) and the actual punchline P is a colimit colim(S'), then the humor H(J) = d(lim(S), colim(S')), where d is a metric on the category of punchlines. Puns have H close to 0 (the punchline is near the expected resolution). Absurdist humor has H large (the punchline is in a completely different category). The universal property of jokes: a joke J is universal if for any other joke J' with the same setup, there is a unique natural transformation J => J'. The funniest jokes are universal — they are the terminal objects in the category of jokes with a given setup. Test: formalize 100 jokes as category-theoretic objects and compute H(J) for each. Correlate with human funniness ratings. Impact: humor is a colimit. The funnier the joke, the further the punchline is from the expected limit of the setup.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the category Joke: objects are setups (functors from a small category to the category of expectations), morphisms are punchlines (natural transformations between setup functors). The expected punchline is the limit of the setup functor: lim(S) = the most likely continuation given the setup. The actual punchline is a specific morphism P: S -> T where T is the target category. The humor value H(J) = d(lim(S), P) where d is the Kantrovich-Rubinstein distance between the distribution of expected continuations and the actual punchline. For puns: S = 'Why did the chicken cross the road?', lim(S) = 'To get to the other side' (the obvious resolution), P = 'To get to the other side' (same as expected), H = 0 (not funny). For absurdist humor: S = 'Why did the chicken cross the road?', P = 'To assert its existential freedom in a deterministic universe', H = large (the punchline is in a completely different category — philosophy rather than transportation). Universal jokes: a joke J is universal if for any joke J' with setup S, there exists a unique natural transformation J => J'. This means J subverts the setup in the most extreme way possible. Test: formalize jokes as functors, compute limits and colimits, measure humor by distance.
directions.title: The Category Theory of Jokes: Universal Properties of Humor

directions.description: Bach's chorales are the gold standard of Western harmony. But what if we could MEASURE the harmonic complexity using topology? Encode each chord as a point in a 12-dimensional space (one dimension per pitch class). A sequence of chords traces a path in this space. Compute the persistent homology of the point cloud of all chords in a Bach chorale. Conjecture: Bach's chorales have persistent H_1 (1-dimensional cycles) that survive across a wide range of scales, indicating circular harmonic motion (the circle of fifths). In contrast, random chord sequences have H_1 bars that die quickly. The longest H_1 bar in a Bach chorale corresponds to the circle of fifths — the fundamental harmonic cycle. Pop music has shorter H_1 bars (less complex harmonic cycles). Atonal music has no persistent H_1 (no harmonic cycles). Test: compute persistent homology barcodes for 100 Bach chorales, 100 pop songs, and 100 atonal pieces. Verify: Bach has H_1 bars of length > 0.5 (in normalized pitch-class space), pop has bars of length 0.2-0.5, atonal has no persistent H_1. Impact: the topology of music IS its harmonic structure. Bach's genius is literally topological — his music has longer harmonic cycles.
directions.proof_strategy: Encode each chord as a binary vector in {0,1}^12 (pitch class set). Map to R^12 using the Fourier transform: each pitch class k maps to e^{2*pi*i*k/12}, giving a point on the unit circle. A chord maps to the sum of its pitch class vectors, normalized. Compute persistent homology of the point cloud of all chords in a piece using Vietoris-Rips complexes. For Bach: the circle of fifths creates a persistent H_1 cycle because chord progressions follow the circle (C -> G -> D -> A -> E -> B -> F# -> C# -> G# -> D# -> A# -> F -> C). This cycle survives across multiple scales. For pop: the cycle is shorter (typically I -> V -> vi -> IV -> I, a 4-chord loop). For atonal: no persistent cycle. Compute: Rips filtration for epsilon = 0.1, 0.2, ..., 1.0. Measure H_1 bar lengths. Test: verify Bach H_1 bars > 0.5, pop H_1 bars 0.2-0.5, atonal H_1 bars < 0.2.
directions.title: Persistent Homology of Musical Harmony: The Topology of Bach

# Future Directions

## 1. Stable exponents under dependency extraction

**Conjecture.** For a fixed, versioned mathematical corpus, the tail exponent of theorem reuse remains within a narrow interval when dependencies are measured under three distinct policies: direct constant references, transitive references, and references after collapsing definitional expansions.

The key insight is that a scale-free claim is scientifically meaningful only if it is stable under reasonable choices of graph extraction. **Why now?** The structural results separate universal consequences of acyclicity from corpus-dependent statistics, making extraction sensitivity the first falsifiable obstacle.

## 2. Width–depth growth across mathematical domains

**Conjecture.** In each sufficiently large subject area, the minimum number of incomparable statements forced by bounded dependency depth grows superlinearly in the logarithm of corpus size.

The key insight is that topological depth controls antichain width through rank collisions, so domain growth can be studied without assuming a power law. **Why now?** A rigorous finite width–depth mechanism is available, and domain-level rank histograms provide a direct empirical test.

## 3. Robustness is governed by redundancy, not degree alone

**Conjecture.** After controlling for out-degree, the number of internally vertex-disjoint weak dependency paths through a theorem predicts deletion damage substantially better than degree centrality.

The key insight is that dense acyclic order networks can have high-degree vertices yet remain connected after every single deletion; alternate routes, rather than degree alone, determine fragility. **Why now?** The robust total-order family supplies an explicit null model against which articulation-based claims can be compared.

## 4. No universal historical hub list

**Conjecture.** The identity and ordering of the ten most reused named theorems vary substantially across algebra, analysis, topology, and combinatorics, even after normalizing for domain size and theorem age.

The key insight is that global prominence may be an aggregation artifact produced by mixing dependency networks with different vocabularies and foundational conventions. **Why now?** The failure of acyclicity to enforce hubs makes stratified, falsifiable ranking comparisons necessary.

## 5. Rank-conditioned heavy tails

**Conjecture.** If a heavy-tailed reuse law exists, its exponent depends systematically on topological rank: early foundational layers have a heavier out-degree tail than late layers.

The key insight is that a single global exponent discards the hierarchy that every finite acyclic dependency network necessarily possesses. **Why now?** Canonical ancestor ranks provide a principled stratification for testing whether the apparent tail is structural or a mixture of heterogeneous layers.

directions.description: The Galois group of a random polynomial over Q is S_n with probability 1. This is the Hilbert irreducibility theorem in probabilistic form. But what about random polynomials over finite fields? For f in F_p[x] of degree n chosen uniformly at random, the Galois group is S_n with probability approaching 1 as p grows. Conjecture: the probability that Gal(f) is NOT S_n is O(p^{-1/2}) for fixed n, and the exceptional cases concentrate at polynomials with discriminant zero or small Galois groups. More precisely, P(Gal(f) != S_n) = c_n / sqrt(p) + O(1/p) where c_n depends only on n. For n=2: P(Gal(f) != S_2) = P(discriminant = 0) = 1/p. For n=3: P(Gal(f) != S_3) = P(f has a rational root) = 3/p + O(1/p^2). Test: enumerate all monic polynomials of degree n over F_p for small p and n, compute Galois groups, verify P(Gal != S_n) ~ c_n / sqrt(p). Impact: random polynomials have maximal Galois groups — algebraic randomness is generic.
directions.proof_strategy: For a random monic polynomial f(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + ... + a_0 over F_p, the Galois group is a subgroup of S_n. Compute P(Gal(f) = S_n) by counting. For n=2: Gal(f) = S_2 unless discriminant = a_1^2 - 4*a_0 = 0, which happens for p choices of a_1 (each gives one a_0), so P = 1 - p/p^2 = 1 - 1/p. For n=3: Gal(f) != S_3 iff f has a rational root (3 choices of root, each determines f) or Gal = A_3 (discriminant is a square). Count both cases. For general n: use the fact that random permutations have cycle structure converging to the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution. The Galois group is S_n unless there is an 'obvious' factorization, which happens with probability O(1/p). Test: implement in Lean 4 + Python. For p=2..100 and n=2..6, enumerate all monic polynomials, compute factorizations, estimate P(Gal != S_n).
directions.title: Stochastic Galois Theory: Random Permutations Have Generic Galois Groups

# Future Directions: Algebraic Geometry of Morphogenetic Surrogates

## 1. Interaction-hypergraph degree law

For affine spatial modes coupled by a polynomial interaction law, the degree of the resulting concentration surrogate should equal the maximum cardinality of an active interaction hyperedge whose coefficient does not cancel in the leading homogeneous part. This is falsifiable by constructing mode families with controlled leading coefficients and comparing the predicted and observed degrees.

The key insight is that interaction order, rather than mode count, controls algebraic degree.

Why now? The two-mode product has exact degree two, while all pairwise interactions among three affine modes still have degree at most two, isolating the missing structural variable.

## 2. Stability of conic nodal topology under algebraic perturbation

A nonsingular compact conic nodal component should persist, with unchanged isotopy type, under every sufficiently small coefficient perturbation that avoids the discriminant locus. Quantitative bounds should relate coefficient distance from the discriminant to the size of the permitted perturbation.

The key insight is that topology changes at singularities, not merely when reaction parameters vary.

Why now? Exact radial bounds and explicit points provide a controlled base case from which coefficient-space stability can be tested.

## 3. Hilbert-sixteenth bounds for finite-mode morphogenetic models

For a degree-d polynomial surrogate arising from finitely many spatial modes, the number of compact planar nodal components should satisfy the Harnack bound, and biologically realizable interaction laws should occupy a strict subregion of the corresponding Hilbert-sixteenth configuration space. This predicts both an absolute topological ceiling and additional reaction–diffusion restrictions.

The key insight is that algebraic degree supplies a universal component bound, while kinetics may impose sharper realizability constraints.

Why now? The conic genus calculation establishes the first degree-genus checkpoint, and the interaction-degree law offers a route to higher-degree tests.

## 4. Singular-limit classification of stripe and spot transitions

Within polynomial finite-mode surrogates, every generic transition between a compact spot component and an unbounded stripe branch should cross the real discriminant hypersurface through an ordinary node or isolated acnode. Higher singularities should occur only in positive-codimension parameter families.

The key insight is that morphological transitions can be organized by the singularity theory of parameterized algebraic curves.

Why now? The radial and hyperbolic models exhibit the two endpoint geometries explicitly, making their intervening discriminant crossings concrete and experimentally accessible.

# Future Directions: Chromatic Thresholds and Social-Network Palettes

## 1. Clique minors as chromatic vanishing certificates

**Conjecture.** If a finite graph contains a complete graph on `t` vertices as a minor, then its chromatic counting function vanishes at every nonnegative palette size below `t`. Conversely, determine natural minor-closed graph classes on which this vanishing pattern forces a complete `t`-minor.

The key insight is that Hadwiger-type structure can be phrased as an interval of forced zeros rather than only as a lower bound on a chromatic number.

**Why now?** The exact minimal-positive-value characterization isolates the zero interval that must be controlled, while deletion–contraction offers a natural mechanism for tracking it through graph reductions.

## 2. Complexity of emotional-threshold detection

**Conjecture.** For every fixed `k ≥ 3`, deciding whether the emotional chromatic number of a finite network is at most `k` remains computationally equivalent, under polynomial reductions, to deciding whether its chromatic counting function is positive at `k`; this equivalence persists for succinctly represented networks and preserves natural approximation gaps.

The key insight is that the semantic threshold and the algebraic positivity test are exactly the same decision boundary above the emotional floor.

**Why now?** The threshold equivalence identifies a precise bridge on which reductions, parameterized algorithms, and counting-versus-decision separations can be compared without changing the underlying instances.

## 3. High-girth networks with unbounded emotional diversity

**Conjecture.** For every pair of integers `g ≥ 3` and `r ≥ 3`, there is a finite network with no cycle shorter than `g` whose emotional chromatic number exceeds `r`; moreover, such examples can be chosen so that the first positive chromatic evaluation occurs sharply after a quantitatively long zero interval.

The key insight is that local tree-like friendship geometry need not constrain the global positivity threshold of proper emotion assignments.

**Why now?** The minimal-positive-value law turns the classical high-girth/high-chromatic phenomenon into a testable statement about an explicit sequence of vanishing evaluations.

## 4. Stability of friendship-network assignment counts

**Conjecture.** Among graphs formed from `n` triangles by identifying vertices while keeping a connected triangle-intersection pattern, the windmill graph extremizes the ratio between the number of six-emotion assignments and the number of minimum-palette assignments; characterize all equality cases.

The key insight is that the windmill’s independent outer pairs produce the exact ratio `2 · 10^n`, suggesting that overlap geometry controls a multiplicative entropy loss.

**Why now?** Closed formulas are available at both the minimum palette and the six-emotion palette, providing a calibrated baseline against which more complicated triangle gluing patterns can be tested.

directions.description: Sudoku is a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). Random Sudoku instances exhibit a phase transition: for n^2 x n^2 grids, the probability of having a solution drops from ~1 to ~0 around a critical density of pre-filled cells. Conjecture: the phase transition occurs at density d_c(n) = (n^2 - 1) / n^2, independent of the specific constraint structure. For standard 9x9 Sudoku (n=3): d_c = 8/9 ≈ 0.889. For 4x4 Sudoku (n=2): d_c = 3/4 = 0.75. For 16x16 (n=4): d_c = 15/16 ≈ 0.9375. The 'hardness' of random Sudoku peaks at the phase transition: instances with density near d_c take exponentially longer to solve than easy (low density) or trivial (high density) instances. Conjecture: the computational hardness of Sudoku at the phase transition is O(exp(n^2)) for backtracking algorithms, matching the theoretical prediction for CSPs at criticality. Test: generate random Sudoku instances at varying densities, measure solver time, and verify the phase transition at d_c. Impact: Sudoku hardness is not about 9x9 grids — it is about the phase transition structure of constraint satisfaction.
directions.proof_strategy: Define random Sudoku(G, d) as a G x G grid with d * G^2 cells pre-filled uniformly at random, subject to the constraint that the pre-filled cells are consistent (no two same numbers in the same row/column/box). For n^2 x n^2 grids: G = n^2. The density d = (# pre-filled) / G^2. Phase transition: P(solvable) as a function of d. For n=2 (4x4): d_c = 3/4. For n=3 (9x9): d_c = 8/9. Theoretical basis: the number of solutions of an empty G x G grid is S(G). Adding a constraint reduces the solution count by approximately S(G)/G. At density d, the number of solutions is approximately S(G) * (1 - 1/G)^{d*G^2} ≈ S(G) * exp(-d*G). This is > 0 when d < (ln S(G))/G ≈ (G-1)/G = d_c. Hardness: at density d near d_c, the expected number of backtracks is exp(O(G)). Test: generate 10000 random Sudoku instances at each density from 0.5 to 0.99, solve with backtracking, measure time, verify phase transition at d_c.
directions.title: The P vs NP of Sudoku: Phase Transitions in Constraint Satisfaction

directions.description: Anyon braiding in topological quantum computing gives unitary matrices from the braid group B_n. The Jones representation rho_k: B_n -> U((k-1)(n-1)+1) at root of unity e^{2*pi*i/k} is conjectured to be universal for quantum computation when k >= 3 and n >= 4. Conjecture: the set of all braids in B_4 under the Jones representation at k=5 generates a dense subgroup of SU(3). More precisely, the image rho_5(B_4) is an infinite subgroup of SU(3) that is not contained in any proper closed subgroup. This means that topological quantum computing with Fibonacci anyons (k=5) is universal: any unitary in SU(3) can be approximated to arbitrary precision by braiding 4 anyons. The key: the Jones representation at k=5 gives 3x3 matrices, and the braid generators sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 generate a dense subgroup of SU(3). Test: compute the Jones representation at k=5 for B_4, verify that sigma_1 * sigma_2 * sigma_3 has infinite order, and check that the group generated by sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 is dense in SU(3) by the Solovay-Kitaev theorem. Impact: braiding anyons is universal for quantum computation. The braid group B_4 at k=5 is a quantum gate set.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the braid group B_n = <sigma_1, ..., sigma_{n-1} | sigma_i * sigma_j = sigma_j * sigma_i for |i-j| > 1, sigma_i * sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i = sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i * sigma_{i+1}>. The Jones representation at root of unity q = e^{2*pi*i/k}: for k=5, q = e^{2*pi*i/5}, the representation rho_5: B_4 -> SU(3). Compute the matrices: sigma_1 = rho_5(sigma_1), sigma_2 = rho_5(sigma_2), sigma_3 = rho_5(sigma_3). These are 3x3 unitary matrices. Verify: (1) sigma_i * sigma_j = sigma_j * sigma_i for |i-j| > 1, (2) sigma_i * sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i = sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i * sigma_{i+1}. Check density: compute sigma_1 * sigma_2 * sigma_3 and verify it has infinite order (the trace is not a root of unity). Apply the Solovay-Kitaev theorem: if the group generated by sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 contains a non-commuting pair and is infinite, then it is dense in SU(3). Test: implement in Python using numpy, compute the Jones representation matrices, verify the braid relations, and check density by approximating random SU(3) matrices.
directions.title: Topological Quantum Compiling: Braid Groups as Universal Gates
